chunks: Draw the NPN BJT symbol. The question: Draw a NPN/BJT symbol.
The NPN transistor symbol is a small picture with three leads: base, collector and emitter. The key detail is the arrow on the emitter.
For an NPN, the arrow points out of the transistor, away from the base.
Getting the arrow right is the whole skill, because it tells you which type it is and which way current flows.
Picture a small sideways fork. The base is a vertical bar with a lead coming in from the left. Two slanted lines leave the bar on the right, like a "V" opening sideways.
The top one goes up to the collector. The bottom one goes down to the emitter, and it carries the arrow. If you can see that shape, you can draw it.
The picture says nothing about the inside of the part, only the connections.
The emitter arrow points out of the NPN (Not Pointing iN) and into the PNP.
In an NPN, I B and I C flow in and I E flows out; in the PNP everything reverses, with I E flowing in and I B , I C flowing out.
The currents satisfy I E equals I C plus I B in both cases.
Base (B): the control lead. A small current here controls a large current. Collector (C): the lead that collects the main current, normally connected toward the supply.
Emitter (E): the lead the current leaves from, normally toward ground. It carries the arrow. NPN: the type with N, P, N layers. The base is the P layer.
Conventional current: the direction positive charge flows, from plus to minus.
Here is the smallest version in words. Draw a vertical bar and add a base lead to its left side.
Draw one slanted line up and right to the collector, and one down and right to the emitter. Put an arrowhead on the emitter line pointing away from the bar. Label B, C and E.
The arrow is the base-emitter diode, pointing from P to N. That is the whole idea.
"The BJT symbol is a base bar with the base lead on one side, and two angled lines on the other: collector at the top and emitter at the bottom. The emitter has an arrow.
For an NPN the arrow points out, away from the base, because it's the base-emitter diode direction, P to N. For a PNP the arrow points in.
Current goes into the collector and base and out of the emitter for an NPN, so I E equals I C plus I B ."
